# Optimization notes

Work began at approximately 23:24 CDT on October 8, 2026. The hard stop is
01:24 CDT on October 9. All GPU experiments ran sequentially, offline, using
the supplied Python environment.

## Kept changes and measurements

The first passing commit combines Q/K/V projections and gate/up projections,
prefills short prompts in one pass, computes only the final query and MLP in
the final layer when logits are needed, skips unused final-layer output during
intermediate prefill chunks, retains MLX's allocation cache during prefill,
and avoids generating a discarded token after the requested continuation.
Weights and KV states remain BF16. Combined projection weights are derived
once from model weights; no request activations or KV states are reused.

`tools/bench.py --scenarios ttft16 ttft256 ctx512 --repeats 2` measured:

| Scenario | TTFT ratio | Decode ratio | Request ratio |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| ttft16 | 1.260 | 1.012 | 1.187 |
| ttft256 | 1.172 | 0.988 | 1.151 |
| ctx512 | 1.139 | 1.003 | 1.026 |

The full supplied correctness check passed for this commit. Median RMS error
ratio was 1.001, p99 maximum error ratio 0.991, and p99 margin error ratio
0.874. Both long-prompt generation tests matched all 32 reference tokens.

## Experiments

- Fused residual addition and RMS normalization: dropped. A sequential paired
  microbenchmark showed essentially unchanged prefill and slightly worse
  synchronous decode. The stock RMS kernel also rounds normalized values to
  BF16 before multiplying by normalization weights; preserving this step is
  necessary when replacing it.
- Compiled prefill plus fused Q/K normalization, RoPE and layout conversion:
  aggregate numerical metrics passed, but the largest FP32 regret exceeded
the check's noise bound (0.3989 versus 0.3355). Not committed.

Compiled prefill alone passed with the same numerical metrics as the first
commit. Its two-repeat process-isolated benchmark measured TTFT ratios 1.297
(16), 1.249 (64), 1.120 (256), and 1.158 (1024). The synchronous paired
comparison showed its clearest incremental benefit at 64 tokens (30.5 to
28.2 ms); larger prefills remain dominated by GPU computation. Compilation
reuses execution graphs, not request data.

For prefills longer than 64 tokens, the final layer now projects Q only for
the last token, and omits Q entirely in intermediate prefill chunks. This
passed the supplied check with unchanged metrics. Paired synchronous forward
timings fell from 84.5 to 83.8 ms at 256 and 343.5 to 340.9 ms at 1024.
The two-repeat supplied benchmark measured TTFT ratios 1.407 (256), 1.059
(1024), and 1.012 (4096). These small incremental savings are within the
variation between separate benchmark sessions; the final table uses one
final measurement session instead of selecting the best historical ratios.

Chunked long requests reserve their rounded BF16 KV capacity on the first
update instead of repeatedly allocating and concatenating larger buffers.
The supplied correctness check again passed with unchanged metrics and both
long continuations matching. A one-repeat supplied benchmark measured
TTFT/decode ratios 1.011/1.005 at 4096 and 1.019/1.011 at 32768.

A custom small-row projection uses 16x32 output tiles, 16-wide K blocks,
FP32 simdgroup matrix accumulation, and BF16 inputs/outputs. It replaces only
16-row, 1024-feature packed QKV and gate/up matmuls; other shapes stay native.
Sampled 1024-wide products matched MLX bit-for-bit. The complete paired
16-token forward improved from 23.1 to 19.2 ms, and the supplied three-repeat
benchmark measured 39.08 versus 50.80 ms TTFT (ratio 1.300). The full supplied
check passed with unchanged metrics. Wider output tiles and larger K blocks
were slower; 64-row and narrower-output projections remain native.

At 512 or more prefill rows, native separate Q/K/V and gate/up projections
are retained instead of packed GEMMs. In paired tests this saved about 1%
at 1024, 2048 and 4096, while separating at 256 was slower. The supplied
two-repeat benchmark measured TTFT ratios 1.091 at 1024 and 1.026 at 4096.
The full supplied correctness check again passed with unchanged metrics.

Additional discarded experiments:

- Fixed-capacity, masked, compiled decode: matched the passing numerical
  metrics in an instrumented copy of the checker, including both long tests.
  Process-isolated decode ratios were 0.988 at 512 and 0.990 at 4096, so it
  was discarded despite a favorable synchronous microbenchmark.
- Combining Q/K normalization with native RMS normalization, a broadcast
  multiply and a single RoPE call: slightly slower in paired measurements.
- Retiling the installed NAX attention source: output disagreed with native
  attention; discarded before integrating into the engine.
- Shape-independent prefill graphs: MLX 0.32.1 cannot infer the relevant
  Split/Slice output shapes. Shape-specialized compiled graphs are retained.
- CPU/GPU projection splitting: one standalone gate/up shape improved, but
  the complete forward slowed from 755 to 930 ms at 2048 and from 1856 to
  2227 ms at 4096. Discarded; all retained computation stays on the GPU.
- Prefill chunk sizes 1024, 2048, 4096 and 8192: only roughly 1% differences
  at 4096 and 9000 in a quick sequential scan. The default remains 2048.

## Final scenario measurements and remaining headroom

To be completed after final validation and process-isolated measurements.

## Time allocation

To be completed at hand-back.

         for e,records in row['results'].items()}
    ratios={k:med['mlx-lm'][k]/med['engine'][k] for k in med['engine']}
    if sid.startswith('ctx'):score=math.sqrt(ratios['ttft']*ratios['decode'])
    elif sid.startswith('req'):score=ratios['request']

import json, math, statistics
from pathlib import Path

rows=json.loads(Path('.tmp/final_short.json').read_text())
rows+=json.loads(Path('.tmp/final_long.json').read_text())
order=['ttft16','ttft64','ttft256','ttft1024','ctx512','ctx4096','ctx32768','req256x256']
summary=[]
for sid in order:
    row=next(r for r in rows if r['scenario']==sid)
    med={e:{k:statistics.median(v[k] for v in records)
            for k in ['ttft','decode','request'] if records[0][k] is not None}
         for e,records in row['results'].items()}
    ratios={k:med['mlx-lm'][k]/med['engine'][k] for k in med['engine']}
    if sid.startswith('ctx'):score=math.sqrt(ratios['ttft']*ratios['decode'])
    elif sid.startswith('req'):score=ratios['request']
    else:score=ratios['ttft']
    summary.append(dict(scenario=sid,repeats=len(row['results']['engine']),
                        median_seconds=med,ratios=ratios,scored_ratio=score))
    print(sid,' '.join(f'{k}={v:.6f}' for k,v in ratios.items()),f'score={score:.6f}',flush=True)
overall=math.exp(statistics.mean(math.log(s['scored_ratio']) for s in summary))

item.stdout:
# Task: make this inference engine faster than mlx-lm

You have a working engine, `engine/engine.py`, that runs Qwen3-0.6B (BF16) on this MacBook Air M4 GPU
with MLX and currently behaves exactly like stock mlx-lm. Make it as fast as you can on the scenarios
below, then hand it back. Its speed will be measured afterwards, independently, against stock mlx-lm.

## Scenarios (equal weight)

TTFT at prompt 16, 64, 256, 1024 tokens; TTFT and decode time per token at contexts 512, 4096 and
32768 (129 tokens generated); whole-request time for 256 prompt + 256 generated tokens.
Batch 1, greedy decoding, fixed number of generated tokens (EOS ignored), token IDs only.

Score: for each of the 8 scenarios, the geometric mean of its speed ratios vs mlx-lm (TTFT; TTFT and
decode for the three contexts; whole request for 256+256); overall, the geometric mean over the 8.

## Rules

- Same mathematics: BF16 weights and BF16 KV cache, the same model function. You may change the
  implementation freely — fusion, kernel rewrites (e.g. `mx.fast.metal_kernel`), scheduling, memory
  layout, summation order, removing work whose result is never used. No quantization, no lower
  precision, no speculative decoding, no approximate or sparse attention, no caching across requests.
- `python tools/check.py` must print PASS for the engine you hand back (numerical error must stay at
  mlx-lm's BF16 noise level). The evaluation applies the same criteria with other prompts, and also
  checks every timed request's generated tokens (up to 32768-token prompts) against mlx-lm's with the
  rule in check.py part 3; a scenario that breaks it counts as no speed-up.
- Keep the API in `engine/engine.py`'s docstring unchanged; the evaluation calls exactly that API.
- Everything the engine needs must live in `engine/` (Python modules, kernel sources, tables) and be
  committed: the evaluation copies only `engine/` from your last commit and imports `engine/engine.py`.
  Do not write files at run time; keep no state between processes.
- Work only inside this directory. Do not read or search other directories on this computer and do not
  use the internet; the installed Python packages (MLX, mlx-lm and their sources) may be read.
- One GPU, one machine: do not run two GPU benchmarks at the same time.

## Budget

About 2 hours of wall-clock time from now (hard stop at 2026-10-09 01:24). Plan for it: the engine as
of your last git commit before the stop is what gets evaluated.

- Commit (`git add -A && git commit -m "..."`) after every change that improves speed **and** passes
  `tools/check.py`. Never leave the last commit in a failing state.
- If you run out of ideas early, stop early.

## Materials

- `docs/HARDWARE.md` — calibrated hardware numbers for this machine.
- `docs/BASELINE.md` — stock mlx-lm timings on the scenarios.

## Tools

- `tools/check.py` — API + numerical check, including long prompts (~2-5 min). PASS required.
- `tools/bench.py --scenarios ... --repeats N` — process-isolated timing vs mlx-lm, thermally gated.
  Prints mlx-lm / engine ratios (> 1 = faster).
- `tools/profile_ops.py` — where time goes inside prefill and decode, vs matmuls and attention alone.
- `tools/platform_state.py` — thermal / power / sleep state of the machine.
- Python: `/Users/aeilot/Developer/research/roofline-inference/.venv-vllm-metal/bin/python` (MLX 0.32.1, mlx-lm 0.32.0).

## Hand-back

Before the deadline, write `NOTES.md`:
1. Each change you kept, with the measured effect (from `tools/bench.py`), and changes you tried and dropped.
2. For every scenario: your final measured ratio vs mlx-lm, and your estimate of how much faster than
   mlx-lm the best possible level-A implementation on this machine could be, with a one-line reason.
3. Where you spent your time (rough percentages by area: e.g. decode matmuls, prefill attention, scheduling, …).
# Hardware calibration — MacBook Air M4 (Mac16,13), 24 GB

Measured with custom Metal/MLX micro-benchmarks, 2026-10-04..07. Best observed values in short
windows ("burst"), cool machine, on AC power. These are calibrations, not guaranteed ceilings.

## GPU (10 cores, unified memory)

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| DRAM read bandwidth, GPU alone | 102.7 GB/s (datasheet 120) |
| DRAM read, CPU alone / CPU + GPU together | 46–54 / 89.6–92.0 GB/s (both together never beat GPU alone) |
| BF16 compute, scalar FMA chain | 3.68 TFLOP/s |
| BF16 compute, register-only simdgroup matrix (MMA) loop | 3.44–3.56 TFLOP/s |
| On-chip L2 + SLC (read knee) | ~12 MiB; reads ~230 GB/s up to 2.4 MiB |
| DRAM latency | ~290 ns |
| Concurrency for 90% of bandwidth / compute | ~1k / ~32k threads |
| Dependent-kernel fixed cost (GPU) | 2.44 µs per kernel |

MLX causal attention (`mx.fast.scaled_dot_product_attention`, 2048 queries, 2k–32k keys): 2.5–2.8 TFLOP/s.
MLX decode attention (1 query, 4k–32k keys, 28 layers): 84–96 GB/s.

## CPU

4 performance + 6 efficiency cores; Accelerate SGEMM ~1.9 TFLOP/s FP32 in bursts. Under sustained
concurrent GPU load the CPU matrix throughput dropped to ~0.7 TFLOP/s (shared power budget).

## Measurement hygiene on this machine

- Fanless: sustained load throttles. 4k-token TTFT went from 1.9 s to 3.1 s after back-to-back runs.
  Compare engines only within one measurement session, interleaved, with cool-down between runs.
- `pmset -g therm` reports nothing useful here. `tools/platform_state.py` reads the OS thermal state
  (0 = nominal), AC power and sleep markers; `tools/bench.py` already waits for state 0.
- After ~1–2 s idle the GPU clocks down; the first request after idle pays ~30–40 ms extra (any engine).
- Keep the machine on AC power with the lid open; a closed lid forces sleep.
- MLX work is asynchronous: synchronize the right stream before reading a timer.
# Optimization notes

Work began at approximately 23:24 CDT on October 8, 2026. The hard stop is
01:24 CDT on October 9. All GPU experiments ran sequentially, offline, using
the supplied Python environment.

## Kept changes and measurements

The first passing commit combines Q/K/V projections and gate/up projections,
prefills short prompts in one pass, computes only the final query and MLP in
the final layer when logits are needed, skips unused final-layer output during
intermediate prefill chunks, retains MLX's allocation cache during prefill,
and avoids generating a discarded token after the requested continuation.
Weights and KV states remain BF16. Combined projection weights are derived
once from model weights; no request activations or KV states are reused.

`tools/bench.py --scenarios ttft16 ttft256 ctx512 --repeats 2` measured:

| Scenario | TTFT ratio | Decode ratio | Request ratio |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| ttft16 | 1.260 | 1.012 | 1.187 |
| ttft256 | 1.172 | 0.988 | 1.151 |
| ctx512 | 1.139 | 1.003 | 1.026 |

The full supplied correctness check passed for this commit. Median RMS error
ratio was 1.001, p99 maximum error ratio 0.991, and p99 margin error ratio
0.874. Both long-prompt generation tests matched all 32 reference tokens.

## Experiments

- Fused residual addition and RMS normalization: dropped. A sequential paired
  microbenchmark showed essentially unchanged prefill and slightly worse
  synchronous decode. The stock RMS kernel also rounds normalized values to
  BF16 before multiplying by normalization weights; preserving this step is
  necessary when replacing it.
- Compiled prefill plus fused Q/K normalization, RoPE and layout conversion:
  aggregate numerical metrics passed, but the largest FP32 regret exceeded
  the check's noise bound (0.3989 versus 0.3355). Not committed.

Compiled prefill alone passed with the same numerical metrics as the first
commit. Its two-repeat process-isolated benchmark measured TTFT ratios 1.297
(16), 1.249 (64), 1.120 (256), and 1.158 (1024). The synchronous paired
comparison showed its clearest incremental benefit at 64 tokens (30.5 to
28.2 ms); larger prefills remain dominated by GPU computation. Compilation
reuses execution graphs, not request data.

For prefills longer than 64 tokens, the final layer now projects Q only for
the last token, and omits Q entirely in intermediate prefill chunks. This
passed the supplied check with unchanged metrics. Paired synchronous forward
timings fell from 84.5 to 83.8 ms at 256 and 343.5 to 340.9 ms at 1024.
The two-repeat supplied benchmark measured TTFT ratios 1.407 (256), 1.059
(1024), and 1.012 (4096). These small incremental savings are within the
variation between separate benchmark sessions; the final table uses one
final measurement session instead of selecting the best historical ratios.
